slides: Open by separating the intuitive phrase shortest path from the computable object used in this chapter. A geodesic is detected by the metric through zero tangential acceleration, and the same metric data also controls curvature. Point students to the source span and the notebook so they understand that this deck follows the local artifact trail rather than a textbook reproduction.

Use this slide to make the main philosophical move precise: Gaussian curvature is not read from the picture of an embedding alone. The plane and cylinder are visually different in space, but the local first fundamental form can be the same. The sphere changes the radial coefficient, so its curvature is already present inside the metric.

Emphasize that the chapter turns geometry into an initial value problem. In geodesic polar coordinates the same two equations cover the sphere, the plane, and the hyperbolic plane once f is chosen. The plotted curves are useful, but the more important evidence is the tiny drift in speed and angular momentum.

Present the triangle identity as a measuring device for curvature. The spherical example has angle excess equal to positive area because K is positive, while the hyperbolic example has angle defect. This lets students see why triangle angle sums are a diagnostic of the surrounding metric rather than a Euclidean constant.

Now widen the triangle budget from one cell to a whole closed surface. The cancellation along shared edges is the important proof idea, because it leaves only vertex deficits and the combinatorial quantity V minus E plus F. The table gives two sanity checks: a tetrahedral sphere and a flat triangular torus.

This is the computational heart of the comparison between constant curvature geometries. Ask students to watch the same radial metric template produce three different circle growth laws. Near zero all three circumferences look Euclidean; farther out, positive curvature suppresses growth and negative curvature accelerates it.

Connect the angle of parallelism back to the hyperbolic metric instead of treating it as a historical curiosity. The distance a from a line determines a limiting angle, and the formula decays monotonically. The table identities are useful checks because they express the same angle through exponential and hyperbolic functions.

Use the pseudosphere as a warning against overinterpreting a model. The parametrized surface has K equal to negative one on the rendered regular part, so it realizes local hyperbolic behavior. But the cusp edge is not incidental: it prevents the surface from serving as a complete embedded copy of the hyperbolic plane.

The lab reverses the usual direction of the formulas. Instead of starting with curvature and drawing circles, it samples circle circumference, reconstructs f, and estimates K from minus f double prime over f. This gives a practical reason to care about circle growth and explains why numerical checks exclude unstable boundary samples.

Close by making the chapter feel like one connected proof rather than a list of formulas. Metric coefficients produce Christoffel symbols, which produce the geodesic ODE. The radial function controls both curvature and circle growth, while triangle budgets aggregate to Euler-Poincare. The artifacts audit each link in that chain.
